item.title: Structure-Aware Placement and Routing of Multi-Controlled Toffoli on Bivariate Bicycle Code Architectures
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Exploiting binary-tree decomposition structure reduces inter-module instructions by up to 16.02% over sequential first-fit placement; grid module layouts reduce them by up to 23.7% relative to linear topologies for multi-controlled Toffoli execution via direct |CCZ⟩ state injection.

Grade 0.459 · 3.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum LDPC codes and low-overhead fault tolerance” · Anik Basu Bhaumik, Suman Dutta, Siyi Wang, Anupam Chattopadhyay

Figure

Comparison of linear versus grid modular bivariate bicycle code layouts, highlighting magic-state factory module placement among regular logical modules.

Asks

How can multi-controlled Toffoli gates be efficiently placed and routed on bivariate bicycle quantum low-density parity-check modular architectures to minimize inter-module communication overhead and execution error?

Before

was sequential first-fit placement on linear bivariate bicycle code architectures (Yoder et al. 2025)

But

Ommits magic-state factory distillation error, models circuit failure as independent Poisson-distributed instruction faults, and evaluates error metrics strictly on linear architectures.

Tools

[[144, 12, 12]] bivariate bicycle code · tree-based subtree co-location · Bicycle-ISA error estimator bicycle_numerics · CCZ magic state injection

Code. https://github.com/qiskit-community/bicycle-architecture-compiler

Abstract

The multi-controlled Toffoli (MCT) gate is a fundamental primitive in quantum circuit design, with applications in quantum arithmetic, cryptanalysis, and algorithmic implementations. Being a high-level logical operation, the efficient decomposition of MCT gates into lower-level netlists has remained a major optimization challenge for decades. While emerging quantum error-correcting codes such as bivariate bicycle (BB) codes drastically reduce fault-tolerance overhead, realizing non-Clifford circuits on modular BB-code architectures introduces complex compilation bottlenecks governed by inter-module routing, factory density, and layout. Consequently, the mapping of MCT gates onto BB-code architectures remains relatively unexplored. In this paper, we overcome these challenges by mapping optimal-Toffoli-depth MCT decompositions (Dutta et al., PRA, 2025) onto BB-code-based fault-tolerant architectures via direct |CCZ ⟩ state injection from an external magic state factory. We introduce a targeted placement strategy that exploits the binary-tree structure of MCT decompositions to co-locate interacting subtrees. This approach reduces inter-module instruction counts by up to 16.02% compared to a naive sequential first-fit placement. We also evaluate the impact of factory placement across different topologies, demonstrating that grid-based layouts yield up to a 23.7% reduction in inter-module instructions relative to linear architectures (Yoder et al., arXiv, 2025). Finally, we validate the practical viability of our compiled circuits by analyzing aggregate execution errors and logical failure probabilities using the bicycle-ISA error estimator bicycle_numerics provided by the Qiskit community, https://github.com/qiskit-community/bicycle-architecture-compiler.

item.title: Encoding Compact U(1) Gauge Fields in Bosonic Modes with GKP Stabilization
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Encodes compact U(1) lattice gauge fields into one continuous-variable bosonic mode per link by enforcing compactness through a GKP stabilizer, which maps the non-compact line to a circle. Evaluated on a single plaquette, real-time spectroscopy with Γ2→0 extrapolation sharpens the extracted charge-induced twist energy from +1.18% bias at single broadening to −0.04% relative error (0.0126316 vs exact 0.0126361).

Grade 0.387 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Victor Ale, Tommaso Rainaldi, Enrique Rico, Felix Ringer, George Siopsis

Figure

Demodulated spectral power |ildeA(ω)|2 against shifted frequency for single-plaquette QED3 across matter couplings κ. Shows the extracted twist energy peak matching between exact electric-basis and compact encoded continuous-variable simulations.

Asks

How can compact U(1) lattice gauge fields be mapped to continuous-variable bosonic modes without artificial subspace truncation or multi-mode embedding?

Before

Embeds U(1) into pairs of qumodes per link and squeezes onto the circle (Ale et al. 2025).

But

Validated on classical simulations of single-plaquette QED3; exact only at infinite squeezing limit (Δ→0); requires spectral separation Δgap=𝒪(1) between the twist line and satellite excitations.

Tools

Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) stabilizers · Gauss law elimination · controlled trigonometric gates · pair-addition spectroscopy · qunaught ancilla phase estimation

Abstract

Compact lattice gauge theories are formulated in terms of angular variables and integer electric fluxes, while bosonic quantum hardware provides oscillator modes with continuous, unbounded quadratures. We bridge this gap with a one-to-one encoding. After Gauss's law is solved, each remaining gauge degree of freedom is carried by a single oscillator mode, with its interactions built from trigonometric gates, and a Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill (GKP)-type stabilizer provides the compactness that the hardware does not. The encoding becomes exact in the limit of infinite squeezing, and at finite squeezing, the leading imperfections act as small, computable shifts of physical observables rather than uncontrolled leakage. We apply the construction to compact QED₃ and derive the error budget at finite squeezing, characterizing the leading errors in closed form, and showing that they can be corrected, subtracted, or extrapolated away. We construct syndrome-extraction protocols that detect and remove the displacement component of photon loss, delimit the noise it does not reach, compare two choices of dynamical variables, and collect the scaling of mode count, gate count, and measurement cost. A one-plaquette example reproduces the exact compact-rotor dynamics, and real-time spectroscopy with controlled extrapolations recovers the exponentially small energy splitting between charge sectors, the seed of the monopole physics of the theory, at the percent level against its exact value.

item.title: A Dynamic Intermediate Representation for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Programs
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Developed dynamic intermediate representation (IR) treating quantum gates as first-class classical values to unify runtime gate creation, composition, and control in hybrid quantum-classical programs.

Grade 0.371 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Suppressing quantum errors by scaling a surface code logical qubit” · Alex Rice, Chris Heunen, Tobias Grosser

Asks

How to design an intermediate representation that natively expresses dynamic, runtime-dependent quantum operations without static circuit-model limitations?

Before

Static circuit-model intermediate representations restricted dynamic gate choices, runtime adaptation, and measurement-dependent branching to disjoint classical-quantum interfaces.

Tools

dynamic IR design · first-class gate semantics · compiler analysis and transformation passes

Abstract

Quantum compilers typically follow the circuit model, representing programs as fixed sequences of gates. This static view breaks down in hybrid quantum-classical applications, where gate choices depend on runtime data or measurement results. We introduce a new Intermediate Representation (IR) that elevates gates to first-class values, enabling their dynamic creation, composition, and control. This unified representation allows classical computation to steer quantum behaviour, capturing phenomena including stochastic gate selection, adaptive error correction, and measurement-driven computation within a single framework. Case studies in noise modelling, randomised compilation, error correction, and measurement-based quantum computing show that our IR expresses these programs compactly and supports optimisations that were not possible in the circuit model. Evaluation on a benchmark suite of hybrid quantum-classical programs indicates that our IR represents programs compactly and facilitates compiler analysis and transformation.

item.title: Exact learning of quantum noise with tensor networks
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Variational optimization of fault-event probabilities via binary cross-entropy on syndrome and logical-flip data learns noise models matching Google Sycamore independently characterized detector error models within 2% in logical error rate.

Grade 0.368 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Nicola Pancotti, Vedika Saravanan, Krysta Svore

Figure

Logical error rate versus time step over 20 steps of synthetic Brownian drift in noise parameters for two drift amplitudes. Online warm-started learning matches the baseline of a decoder with perfect instantaneous noise knowledge across five independent runs.

Asks

Can quantum error-correction syndrome and logical-observable data collected during memory experiments be used to learn device noise models directly without dedicated characterization runs?

Before

was offline characterization (randomized benchmarking, Pauli channel estimation, sparse Pauli–Lindblad models) requiring separate experiments

But

Demonstrated on distance-3 surface codes with 3 rounds of syndrome extraction; exact tensor-network contraction scales exponentially with decoding graph treewidth.

Tools

variational optimization via binary cross-entropy · tensor-network maximum-likelihood decoder · analytic gradient descent · warm-started online tracking

Abstract

Accurate noise models are essential for high-performance quantum error correction, yet characterizing the noise of a quantum device typically requires dedicated experiments. We present a variational framework that learns the noise model directly from quantum-error-correction syndrome and logical-observable data collected during error-corrected memory experiments. The fault-event probabilities are treated as variational parameters and optimized via gradient descent to minimize the binary cross-entropy between the decoder's predictions and experimental logical-observable outcomes. We prove that this objective is principled rather than ad hoc: a sufficiently expressive noise ansatz attains the information-theoretic minimum logical error rate. We instantiate this framework using a tensor-network decoder, which provides exact maximum-likelihood decoding and analytically differentiable gradients with respect to all noise parameters. Using circuit-level data from Google's Sycamore processor, and starting from an uninformed prior, the optimization recovers noise models whose logical error rates agree to within 2% with those of Google's independently characterized detector error model. The mean squared error between the learned and reference noise parameters shows a clear overall decrease throughout training, confirming that the method recovers physically meaningful noise structure, not merely parameters that happen to decode well. We further demonstrate that the optimization can track device drifts in real time via warm-started updates, maintaining near-optimal decoding performance under synthetically evolving noise without the need for re-characterization. The approach is decoder-agnostic in its formulation and naturally extends to correlated noise models.

item.title: Codes for Quantum Secret Sharing with a Helper
item.description:
Worth a look theory — For single-qubit blind helper stabilizer codes, helper blindness is necessary and sufficient for recovery via one-way LOCC from the helper. All pure multi-qubit helper codes reduce to a coherent quantum one-time pad undone by a controlled unitary with the helper.

Grade 0.368 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum LDPC codes and low-overhead fault tolerance” · Eric Chitambar, Sarah Hagen, David W. Kribs, Zhao Ma, Mike I. Nelson, Andrew Nemec

Figure

Pure quantum secret sharing setup with isometric encoding W and reference system 𝖰~, showing erasure correction and state recovery on any authorized subset S.

Asks

What is the general structure and decodability under LOCC of pure quantum secret sharing codes equipped with a privileged helper?

But

Single-qubit encoded secret. In the stabilizer LOCC-addressable case, requires an odd number of regular parties (unless one party holds multiple shares).

Tools

stabilizer formalism · one-way LOCC · quantum erasure correction · replacer code structure theorem

Abstract

Helper quantum secret sharing is a form of secret sharing defined by its unique access structure. One special fixed party, called the helper, can work together with any other party to fully decode the secret. A blind helper is one who can provide this assistance while not holding any local information about the encoded secret. In this work, we analyze the general structure of QSS helper codes and present new code constructions. We fully characterize the structure of blind helper stabilizer codes and show that for the encoding of a single qubit, recovery is always possible using one-way local operations and classical communication (LOCC) from the helper to the targeted party. Furthermore, we demonstrate how such codes also allow for the helper to target larger subsets of parties by one-way LOCC, enabling them to be authorized to recover the secret. Finally, when each party only holds a qubit, we identify the general form of all helper codes (including non-stabilizer codes) and find that LOCC recovery is only possible in special cases.

item.title: High-Rank Encoding Can Improve Approximate Quantum Error Correction
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Restricting approximate quantum error correction encoders to rank one incurs an infidelity penalty at most quadratic near perfect recovery, Δ≤(s−1−1)ℓs(ε)2 for ε≤s. Higher-rank encoders mapping pure inputs to mixed states are strictly required to attain optimal entanglement fidelity for an explicit noise family arbitrarily close to perfect recovery.

Grade 0.358 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Bikun Li, Liang Jiang

Figure

(a) Infidelity gap bound Δ(ε,s) plotted against infidelity ε for various smallest positive eigenvalues s, showing the quadratic improvement over the prior ε(1−ε) bound. (b) Optimized gap plotted against optimized infidelity across varying logical dimensions dL under a test noise family.

Asks

Can general, higher-rank encoders strictly outperform partial-isometry (rank-one) encoders in approximate quantum error correction without exact-recovery constraints?

Before

Rank-one encoders lose nothing at exact recovery (F=1), but under the earlier bound adapted from Barnum-Knill-Nielsen (1998), replacing an encoder by a partial isometry incurred an infidelity increase up to ε(1−ε), which is linear in ε.

But

Bounds assume completely positive trace-non-increasing (CPTNI) or CPTP maps on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces with dC≥dL; joint optimization is biconvex without analytic global convergence certificates at arbitrary fixed noise.

Tools

Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism · Semidefinite programming (SDP) · Biconvex seesaw optimization · Polar decomposition

Abstract

Conventional quantum-code constructions encode pure logical states as pure code states, but this restriction can sacrifice performance. We show that intrinsic encoding randomness can improve optimal entanglement fidelity. We bound the loss from imposing a rank-one encoder and prove it is at most quadratic near perfect recovery after joint optimization. The optimized advantage survives small noise perturbations. An explicit noise family requires higher-rank encoders arbitrarily close to perfect recovery, with every optimal encoder mapping pure inputs to mixed code states.
